title: PCA · from picture to proof

chapters.question: How do we measure a view?
What can we keep and recover?

slides.title: What is PCA?
slides.action: Rotate one line through a measured cloud. Watch four observations become four scores.
slides.claim: PCA finds new perpendicular axes, ordered by variance. Keeping fewer axes reduces the number of values per observation.

slides.title: One number is a position on a line
slides.action: Select an observation. Link its point, projection, and single stored score.
slides.claim: The point and its score refer to the same observation.

slides.title: Some views lose more than others
slides.action: Compare 45° and 135° with the same scale in both score plots.
slides.claim: A useful projection keeps a large part of the original squared spread.

slides.title: A projection follows a perpendicular
slides.action: Move one point to its closest position on the chosen line.
slides.claim: The line is the axis that we KEEP; the viewing direction is perpendicular to it.

slides.title: What does one score lose?
slides.action: Hide the original points. Reveal the possible points that share a score.
slides.claim: A score cannot recover movement across its axis.

slides.title: Turn the axes, then remove one
slides.action: Switch between two rotated coordinates and one retained coordinate.
slides.claim: Rotation alone loses nothing. Removing a coordinate can lose detail.

slides.title: What will best mean?
slides.action: Compare kept squared spread with squared reconstruction error.
slides.claim: These are two equivalent PCA objectives under the same Euclidean scale.

slides.title: See the whole method once
slides.action: Step through center → find axes → keep scores → reconstruct.
slides.claim: The next chapters explain how to compute this result.

slides.title: Measure change from a shared center
slides.action: Translate the cloud without changing its shape.
slides.claim: The PCA direction describes variation around the mean.

slides.title: Find the center of this cloud
slides.action: Highlight one column and calculate its mean.
slides.claim: Introduce the mean only because we need this center.

steps.why: Add the four values in each column. Divide each sum by four.

slides.title: Move the center to zero
slides.action: Scrub the translation. Keep observation labels fixed.
slides.claim: Subtract the corresponding feature mean from each observation.

steps.why: Subtract the mean of each feature. A is two units right and one unit up from the center.

slides.title: The distances do not change
slides.action: Select two observations before and after translation.
slides.claim: Centering changes the origin, not the relative positions.

steps.why: The two copies of the mean cancel. The difference between observations stays the same.

slides.title: Describe the line with two numbers
slides.action: Rotate a unit arrow. Its horizontal and vertical parts update.
slides.claim: The vector w gives a direction and has length one.

steps.why: The angle sets the direction. The unit length fixes the scale of its scores.

slides.title: Calculate one score
slides.action: Select A. Multiply each centered coordinate by its direction weight.
slides.claim: The dot product gives signed distance along a unit axis.

steps.why: Multiply matching coordinates. Add the two products. A negative score is on the other side of the center.

slides.title: Use one rule for every observation
slides.action: Link each row of Xc to its score in Xc w.
slides.claim: Rows are observations; columns are features. Show the matrix shapes here.

steps.why: Apply the same weights to each row. This matrix product produces all four scores.

slides.title: Keep the ruler length fixed
slides.action: Double the direction length without changing its angle.
slides.claim: Without the unit constraint, scores and variance can grow without limit.

steps.why: Doubling the arrow doubles every score. The variance then becomes four times as large.

slides.title: How spread out are the scores?
slides.action: Compare scores around zero at two angles.
slides.claim: Centered input produces scores whose mean is zero.

steps.why: The centered feature means are zero. Their weighted sum is also zero.

slides.title: Signs cancel; squares do not
slides.action: Switch signed contributions to square areas.
slides.claim: Squaring measures both directions and supports the distance identity used later.

steps.why: Positive and negative scores can cancel. Their squares measure spread on both sides of the center.

slides.title: Give spread a number
slides.action: Add four squared scores and divide by three.
slides.claim: Use sample variance throughout. An optional note explains n−1; changing it to n does not change the best axis.

steps.why: This is sample variance for four centered scores. Its units are square centimeters.

slides.title: Search with a variance curve
slides.action: Rotate the line. Link the angle to a point on the variance curve.
slides.claim: The highest point gives our numerical target. We still need a general method.

steps.why: The graph evaluates this expression for each direction. Next, we derive a way to find its maximum.

slides.title: Open one squared score
slides.action: Reveal each term in (w1 a + w2 b)².
slides.claim: Show the two identical cross-products before replacing them with a factor of two.

steps.why: Write the square as a product of two identical sums.
Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.
The middle products are equal. Add them to get the factor two.

slides.title: Add the same terms across rows
slides.action: Select one observation in the sum. Then group matching terms.
slides.claim: The weights are shared by all observations, so they can leave the sum.

steps.why: Add the expanded square for every observation.
The weights do not depend on the observation. Put them outside their sums.

slides.title: Two familiar sums and one new sum
slides.action: Link the first and last terms to the two feature variances.
slides.claim: The middle sum measures how the two centered features vary together.

steps.why: The two square sums are feature variances. Name the product sum covariance, written as s_ab.

slides.title: Build covariance from signed products
slides.action: Select observations in each quadrant. Flip the second feature.
slides.claim: Same signs give positive products; opposite signs give negative products.

steps.why: Each product is positive in this cloud. Both features tend to lie on the same side of their means.

slides.title: Variance alone cannot tell the tilt
slides.action: Compare two clouds with the same marginal variances and opposite covariance.
slides.claim: The cross-term distinguishes these clouds.

steps.why: Changing the sign of the second feature preserves its squares. It reverses each cross-product.

slides.title: Store the three quantities in S
slides.action: Select a covariance matrix entry to reveal its products.
slides.claim: The diagonal stores variances. Both off-diagonal entries store the same covariance.

steps.why: The matrix stores the three quantities needed to calculate variance in any direction.

slides.title: Compute S with one matrix product
slides.action: Animate a selected row of Xcᵀ meeting a column of Xc.
slides.claim: Transpose and multiplication are compact ways to do the sums we already used.

steps.why: A row meets a column. Multiply matching entries and add.
Divide all four sums by the same sample divisor.

slides.title: Read wᵀ S w from inside out
slides.action: Calculate Sw, then the dot product with w.
slides.claim: The compact formula is exactly the expanded variance expression.

steps.why: First multiply S by w. This gives a two-coordinate vector.
Take its dot product with w. The result is our expanded variance.

slides.title: Check both routes with real numbers
slides.action: Compare direct squared scores with wᵀ S w at any angle.
slides.claim: The two calculations agree because we derived their identity.

steps.why: Transposing a product reverses its order. These are three forms of the same calculation.

slides.title: State the optimization problem
slides.action: Show a unit circle of permitted directions and a variance curve.
slides.claim: Maximize wᵀ S w with wᵀ w = 1.

steps.why: Choose the direction with the largest score variance. Compare only arrows of unit length.

slides.title: What does S do to an arrow?
slides.action: Move w around the unit circle. Show Sw on a common labeled scale.
slides.claim: A matrix is also a rule that maps one vector to another.

steps.why: The same covariance matrix can map a direction arrow to a new arrow.

slides.title: At an optimum, turning cannot help
slides.action: Compare a direction with small clockwise and counterclockwise turns.
slides.claim: The allowed change runs along the circle. At an optimum its first-order gain is zero.

steps.why: The vector t points along a small turn of w. At a stationary direction, this slope is zero.

slides.title: Find the variance slope
slides.action: Differentiate the two-coordinate quadratic one term at a time.
slides.claim: The gradient is (2S11w1+2S12w2, 2S12w1+2S22w2) = 2Sw.

steps.why: A partial derivative changes one coordinate while the other stays fixed.
Use the square rule. The term with only w2 has zero derivative.
Repeat for w2. Symmetry makes the two cross-term coefficients agree.
The gradient collects these two slopes into one vector.

slides.title: Find the constraint direction
slides.action: Differentiate w1²+w2². Show the normal arrow to the circle.
slides.claim: The gradient 2w points outward; allowed small changes point perpendicular to it.

steps.why: This equation describes the circle of permitted directions.
The gradient points outward. A small allowed change is tangent to the circle.

slides.title: Match the two normal directions
slides.action: Align the gradient arrows at a stationary point.
slides.claim: 2Sw = 2λw, so Sw = λw. This finds candidates; it does not yet prove a maximum.

steps.why: At a constrained optimum, the objective gradient has no component along an allowed small change.
Substitute the two gradients that we just calculated.
Divide both sides by two. The multiplier becomes the scale factor of this direction.

slides.title: Name the equation after it appears
slides.action: Compare w and Sw at both stationary directions.
slides.claim: An eigenvector keeps its direction under S. Its eigenvalue is the scale factor.

steps.why: The input arrow q and its image Sq lie on the same line. This defines an eigenvector and its eigenvalue.

slides.title: Find the possible scale factors
slides.action: Subtract λ on the diagonal. Expand the 2×2 determinant.
slides.claim: A nonzero solution requires S−λI to be singular. Explain determinant only here.

steps.why: Move the right side to the left. A nonzero solution requires a singular matrix.
For a two-by-two matrix, the determinant is the diagonal product minus the other product.

slides.title: Solve our two eigenvalues
slides.action: Factor (10/3−λ)²−(8/3)². Link each root to the curve.
slides.claim: The roots are 6 and 2/3.

steps.why: Factor the difference of two squares.
A product is zero when one factor is zero.
These are the two possible scale factors. We order them from largest to smallest.

slides.title: Find and normalize the directions
slides.action: Solve w2=w1 and w2=−w1. Set each vector length to one.
slides.claim: The directions are (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2.

steps.why: Substitute 6 in the first row of the eigenvector equation. Multiply that row by three.
Repeat for 2/3. Divide each direction by its length to make a unit vector.

slides.title: A candidate can be a minimum
slides.action: Select each eigenvector and compare its variance.
slides.claim: The eigenvector equation alone does not choose PC1.

steps.why: A unit eigenvector has variance equal to its eigenvalue. One candidate is the maximum; the other is the minimum.

slides.title: Why are these directions perpendicular?
slides.action: Expand q1ᵀSq2 in two ways and compare.
slides.claim: Symmetry gives (λ1−λ2)q1ᵀq2=0. Distinct eigenvalues imply perpendicular eigenvectors.

steps.why: Apply S to q2 first.
Symmetry lets S act on the other vector.
If the eigenvalues differ, the dot product must be zero. The two directions are perpendicular.

slides.title: Build any unit direction from them
slides.action: Rotate w and show coefficients a and b on the two eigenvectors.
slides.claim: w=aq1+bq2 and a²+b²=1. State the symmetric-matrix basis theorem for higher dimensions.

steps.why: The two unit eigenvectors form perpendicular axes. Every unit direction has coordinates a and b on these axes.

slides.title: Expand variance in the new basis
slides.action: Open four terms. Cancel both cross-terms with orthogonality.
slides.claim: The result is λ1a²+λ2b².

steps.why: Substitute the coordinates of w in the eigenvector basis.
Expand the four products. Replace Sq1 and Sq2 with their eigenvalue forms.
Both cross-terms contain a zero dot product. Each unit vector has squared length one.

slides.title: Prove the largest value wins
slides.action: Move the squared-weight allocation between λ1 and λ2.
slides.claim: A weighted average cannot exceed its largest entry. Equality at q1 proves global optimality.

steps.why: Because λ2 is no larger than λ1, replacing λ2 cannot decrease this expression.
The nonnegative squared weights add to one.
This direction reaches the bound. It is a global maximum, not just a stationary point.

slides.title: What if the eigenvalues tie?
slides.action: Change to an isotropic cloud. Rotate freely.
slides.claim: All directions in a tied eigenspace give the same variance. A unique PC1 is not guaranteed.

steps.why: Equal eigenvalues give the same variance for every direction in their shared space.

slides.title: Find the next component
slides.action: Restrict the next direction to the perpendicular space.
slides.claim: Maximize remaining variance there. In two dimensions the remaining axis is fixed up to sign.

steps.why: The next component must be perpendicular to PC1. In higher dimensions, maximize variance within that remaining space.

slides.title: Read the PCA coordinates
slides.action: Rotate both axes, then relabel the plot as PC1 and PC2.
slides.claim: Loadings describe axes. Scores describe observations.

steps.why: Each column of Q describes an axis. Each row of Z contains the new coordinates of one observation.

slides.title: Check the new covariance
slides.action: Select an entry of QᵀSQ. See the off-diagonal product sum vanish.
slides.claim: The score columns are uncorrelated. This does not generally mean independent.

steps.why: Substitute Z=XcQ and group the covariance matrix.
Orthonormal eigenvectors make the off-diagonal entries zero.

slides.title: Explain the 90 percent
slides.action: Connect eigenvalue bars to the sum of squared centered distances.
slides.claim: 6/(6+2/3)=90%. This is a fraction of variance, not prediction accuracy.

steps.why: The denominator is total variance. The ratio measures retained squared spread.

slides.title: Rebuild an observation from its score
slides.action: Select A. Multiply its score by q1, then add the mean.
slides.claim: The reconstructed point lies on the retained line.

steps.why: Multiply the retained score by its axis. Add the stored mean.
A originally measured (8,7). Its one-score reconstruction has an error in both features.

slides.title: Draw the missing part
slides.action: Show the original vector, projection, and residual as a right triangle.
slides.claim: Orthogonality gives original squared length = kept squared length + lost squared length.

steps.why: The residual e is the difference between the original point and its projection.
The kept vector and residual are perpendicular. Apply the right-triangle identity.

slides.title: Prove the second objective
slides.action: Add the triangle identity across all observations.
slides.claim: Total squared length is fixed, so maximizing kept variance minimizes squared reconstruction error.

steps.why: Add the identity for every observation and move the kept term to the right.
Trace is the sum of the feature variances. The first term does not depend on the direction.
The same direction solves both problems. The errors are perpendicular distances, not vertical regression errors.

slides.title: Recover both coordinates
slides.action: Switch between k=0, k=1, and k=2.
slides.claim: Two orthonormal coordinates recover the original centered vector.

steps.why: Keeping both perpendicular coordinates recovers the original centered vector.

slides.title: Choose how much to keep
slides.action: Set a retained-variance target and select k.
slides.claim: The task determines an acceptable error. A percentage alone does not prove usefulness.

steps.why: The loss uses the sample divisor n−1. Multiply it by n−1 to get the total squared error.

slides.title: Extend from two features to p
slides.action: Keep the top k eigenvalues in a larger spectrum.
slides.claim: For orthonormal W, retained variance is tr(WᵀSW). The top k eigenvectors maximize it; discarded eigenvalues give the loss.

steps.why: W contains k perpendicular unit directions. Define αj as the squared length of the projection of qj into their space.
A projection cannot increase a unit vector length. The sum equals the dimension of the retained space.
Allocate the weight to the largest eigenvalues first. Choosing their eigenvectors reaches this bound.

slides.title: Connect the result to SVD
slides.action: Substitute Xc=UΣVᵀ into S=XcᵀXc/(n−1).
slides.claim: The columns of V are PCA directions. Eigenvalues equal squared singular values divided by n−1.

steps.why: Singular value decomposition factors the centered table. U and V have orthonormal columns in the compact form.
Use UᵀU=I. The diagonal entries are the squared singular values divided by n−1.
SVD gives the same PCA directions without explicitly forming the covariance matrix.

slides.title: Use the axes on a new observation
slides.action: Enter a new observation and apply the training mean and axes.
slides.claim: Fit preprocessing and PCA on training data. Reuse those values for later observations.

steps.why: Keep the training mean and learned directions fixed. New observations do not refit this model.

slides.title: Decide what units mean
slides.action: Change one feature scale, then compare standardization.
slides.claim: Standardization changes the question. It gives each nonconstant feature unit variance.

steps.why: Divide each centered feature by its sample standard deviation. Nonconstant features then have variance one.

slides.title: Large variance is not always useful
slides.action: Reveal a distant observation and then category labels.
slides.claim: Outliers can dominate squared spread. A useful label can lie in a low-variance direction.

slides.title: A line cannot follow every shape
slides.action: Compare a ring with the elongated cloud.
slides.claim: PCA is linear. Two components may be necessary even if a curve has one intrinsic parameter.

slides.title: Change the real notebook data
slides.action: Use native marimo controls to change an observation.
slides.claim: Python recomputes mean, covariance, directions, scores, and reconstruction.

slides.title: Solve a fresh geometric problem
slides.action: Choose a direction for a rotated, unseen cloud before seeing its optimum.
slides.claim: Require a prediction and a reason; then compare with the computed result.

slides.title: Produce the calculation yourself
slides.action: Compute a covariance entry, a score, and a reconstruction for new values.
slides.claim: Record numeric correctness separately from the learner’s written explanation.

slides.title: Teach PCA back in your own words
slides.action: Explain purpose → objective → covariance → eigenvectors → loss.
slides.claim: Use new examples and name one limit. Reopen the exact relevant scene after a miss.

center: The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations. Calculate one mean per feature. Subtract each feature mean from its values. Centered values describe differences from the mean.
score: A vector stores coordinates. A unit vector has length one. Its dot product with a point gives the signed projection score. Multiply matching coordinates, then add.
variance: Variance measures squared spread around a mean. Here the score mean is zero. Add the squared scores and divide by n−1. Using n instead changes the scale but not the best direction.
expansion: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket. In (A+B)², the middle terms are AB and BA. They give 2AB.
covariance: Transpose swaps rows and columns. A matrix product matches one row with one column. Multiply matching entries and add. In XcᵀXc, each entry compares two feature columns.
objective: Xc has n rows and p columns. w has p entries. Xc w has n scores. S has p rows and p columns. wᵀSw is one number.
eigen: A derivative measures local change. A gradient collects one derivative per coordinate. On the unit circle, allowed small changes follow the tangent. At a constrained optimum, the gradient has no tangent component. Sw=λw says that S preserves the line of w.
maximum: The basis theorem and the bound

A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. We use this theorem for higher dimensions. The two-dimensional example can be checked directly. Squared coordinates in this basis are nonnegative and add to one. Their weighted eigenvalue average cannot exceed the largest eigenvalue.
coordinates: Loadings are the feature weights in an axis. Scores are the coordinates of observations on that axis. Sign reversal changes both signs and preserves the same projection. Zero covariance does not generally imply independence.
reconstruction: The squared length of (a,b) is a²+b². A unit-axis projection is zw. Its residual is perpendicular to the axis. Their squared lengths add. Trace means the sum of the diagonal entries.
spectrum: The columns of W are perpendicular unit vectors. WᵀW=I. Projecting onto these k directions gives k scores. Keeping all directions preserves the data. Keeping fewer can lose detail.
geometry: Each letter is one observation. Teal marks the retained axis. The score line shows one number for each observation. Orange marks a lost part. The axis we keep is perpendicular to the direction of a shadow.

notation: The mean of each original feature.
A table of centered observations, one per row.
A candidate direction of unit length.
The score of observation i on w.
A learned unit eigenvector, or PCA direction.
